#127846. Breaking: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?

Breaking: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
  • In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
  • Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.

In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.

Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure.".

The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, noted it was shelving intends to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot.".

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation.".

In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.

Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.

Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.

"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.

China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.

Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security.".

PwC remarked Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.

"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.

With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.

"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.

Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Recent findings suggest that domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).

IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

Sources indicate that in Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000.".

Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.

For Germany, the glitch isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany.".

"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

While trading in a classic book for a digital device may seem sacrilegious, the reading community has wholeheartedly embraced e-readers. Just head over to BookTok, and you'll find a passionate community of Kindle, Kobo, and Boox users.

Industry observers note that when you think of the best e-readers, your first thought is likely an Amazon Kindle; however, this isn't a list of the best Kindles — although we do have a list of those, too. While Kindles are great (especially the latest models) — there's certainly no denying that — you can find a couple of equally wonderful alternatives.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

According to recent reports, so, what is the best e-reader for 2026? I'm regularly testing new e-readers (and tablets) and cycling through different models to stay up to date on the best options available. If you're gearing up to read more books this year, I can recommend a model you'll love.

Sources indicate that and Amazon recently released my newly introduced favorite e-reader. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Black Friday falls on Nov. 27 this year, and the sales started well before then. The best deals are on Kindles, which have some unbeatable prices. The 2024 Kindle Paperwhite is our favorite early Black Friday e-reader deal. It's been on sale for $129.99, knocking $70 off its $199.99 price tag, but there are even more Black Friday Kindle deals in store for both 2024 and 2026 models.

Industry observers note that but what about other e-readers? The best deal outside of Kindles is on the Kobo Libra Colour, which is down to $229.99. That saves you $30 off its MSRP of $259.99. Keep in mind that its $229.99 sale price is $10 more than its previous MSRP of $219.99 (Kobo raised its price earlier this year). However, the Kindle Paperwhite is $20 less than its previous MSRP (it was raised from $149.99 to $199.99 in August 2026).

On Oct. 1, Amazon dropped a redesigned collection of Kindles. We've tested the latest e-readers and named the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition the best overall e-reader.

As of September 2026, we've added the Boox Go 6 to this guide, naming it the best Kindle alternative. We also named the Kindle Paperwhite the best e-reader for the beach (in addition to being the best overall) and named the Durobo Krono the best e-reader for audiobooks.

In August 2026, Amazon increased the price of Kindles. Now the basic Kindle costs $149.99 ($40 increase) and the Kindle Paperwhite costs $199.99 ($40 increase).

Sources indicate that in July 2026, Boox confirmed it was releasing a pocket-sized e-reader, the Picco. After IFA 2026, rumors floated that the Boox Picco would be released in November 2026.

Also in July 2026, Xteink dropped the X4 Pro, a new tiny e-reader with a touchscreen.

As of April 2026, we have included the Durobo Krono and the Xetink X4 e-reader in this guide.

In May 2026, Amazon ceased support for e-readers released in 2012 or earlier, which includes the first generation of Kindle and Kindle Paperwhite.

Also in May 2026, Kobo announced its integration with Storygraph, which syncs your on-device reading progress with the Storygraph app.

Read our full review of the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (2026).

It has been revealed that pretty much everyone: If Amazon is pretty intrinsic to your spending, then going for a Kindle, specifically the Paperwhite Signature Edition, makes the most sense. While we previously saw it as an upgrade pick, the new aluminum casing makes it essential with a sleeker, sturdier case. It turns pages without stuttering, never slowing down when you’re in the thick of the action.

In a recent development, beach readers: It's also the best e-reader for the beach. The screen is vibrant and has adjustable brightness, meaning it can adapt when transitioning from reading in bright sunlight to dimmer indoors. You can adjust the brightness manually or set it to automatically adjust. It also comes with adjustable screen warmth, perfect for evening readers who want to give their eyes a chance to relax. It’s lightweight and fits comfortably in small crossbody bags. Plus, it’s waterproof, keeping it safe from poolside vacations and spilled water bottles in bags.

Recent findings suggest that the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition dethrones the 2024 Kindle Paperwhite as the best overall e-reader. Historically, I've preferred the Paperwhite, finding that the Signature Edition doesn't have enough features to justify its price, but the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition finally fixes that. With a new aluminum case, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition feels like a high-end piece of tech. With a thinner body and square edges, this new Kindle feels more like a smartphone or tablet than it does an e-reader.

It has been revealed that but inside the more advanced chassis is still the same e-reader you love. It's fast with a high-contrast 300 ppi resolution. The matte display is glare-free and easy on the eyes. With adjustable warmth and brightness, you can read with it in bright summer sun at the beach and then turn it down and warm it up when you're in a dim bedroom. And speaking of the beach, its IPX8 rating makes it safe to use in the bath or at the pool.

It is a more expensive e-reader at $249.99, especially compared to the Paperwhite's $199.99, but here's what you get for an extra $50. The upgraded aluminum case makes that $50 nearly worth it compared to the plastic exterior of the Paperwhite, but the Signature Edition also has an ad-free lockscreen, 32GB of storage compared to the Paperwhite's 16GB, wireless charging, auto-adjusting brightness, and best of all, compatibility with the new Kindle Page Turn Cover.

Sources indicate that plus, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition comes in more exciting color options. While the Paperwhite just comes in graphite, the Signature Edition also comes in a stunning seaglass green.

According to recent reports, don't get us wrong, though; we still love the Kindle Paperwhite. If you want to save $50, the next best e-reader you can buy is the basic Kindle Paperwhite. It's still a quick, well-rounded e-reader but doesn't come in fun colors and has lockscreen ads.

Read our full review of the Kobo Clara Colour.

Industry observers note that for those who want an Amazon alternative: If you're just diving into the world of e-readers and not particularly thrilled about Kindles and their Amazon ties, then the Kobo Clara is the right answer. It offers a color display for those who enjoy manga and graphic novels, but it remains speedy with fast processing when turning pages or swapping between books.

Libby users: It's especially great for Libby users, who want seamless integration with books that automatically load into your library as soon as you borrow them. While Kindle's Libby integration only works in the U.S., the Kobo works with Libby no matter where you live.

Recent findings suggest that having tried my hand at more than a dozen e-readers in all shapes, sizes, and brands, I wasn't expecting to be so deeply impressed by the Kobo Clara Colour, but it is a wonderful e-reader. With a 6-inch screen, it's slightly smaller than the Kindle Paperwhite, but it allows you to hold it comfortably for multiple hours at a time without any wrist or arm fatigue.

Industry observers note that in my previous testing with Kobo devices, I've really liked them, but one sticking point is that they're slower than Kindles. Initially, I found that the Kobo Clara kept up with the Paperwhite, but after several months of use, it had a tendency to lag. Compared to Kindles, I had to manually sync the Kobo Clara to get my library books to show up.

Industry observers note that its processing system is otherwise really smart and fixes one of my biggest e-reader pet peeves. When you adjust the font size on a Kindle, the device doesn't recalculate how many pages are in the book, making it inaccurate, so you don't know exactly how many pages you have left in a chapter. The Kobo Clara does recalculate page count accurately for a more exact reading experience. Though, one thing to note: Kobo counts the number of digital pages, whereas Kindle page numbers typically match up with physical book copies.

In a recent development, for the same price as the Kindle Paperwhite, the Kobo Clara offers color displays, something you can't get in the Kindle lineup unless you're willing to spend $250. The colors aren't as bright as you'd experience in a physical book, but they're still vivid enough to enjoy a graphic novel.

The Kobo Clara's biggest downfall is its battery life. It's supposed to last up to 42 days, although many online customers say it averages out at about two weeks. That's quite pathetic in the face of the Kindle's 12-week battery life; however, I'd trade in a better reading experience over a couple weeks of battery life any day.

Read our full review of the Durobo Krono.

According to recent reports, across app readers: If your digital library is sprawling — you have books through Kindle, Kobo, Libby, and Audible — then you need an e-reader that can access all of them. Durobo's Krono e-reader is a compact e-reader that basically functions like a tablet. Most e-readers on this list are Androids, but none have open Android systems that let you download the apps you want, as the Krono does.

Audiobook lovers: For the audiobook lovers, the Durobo Krono also plays audio in addition to transcribing it. With access to the Google Play store available, you can download any app you read on to access your digital library, including Audible, Libro.fm, and Spotify. However, if you have a collection of EPUB files, you can also download them directly to Krono's library.

Sources indicate that having tried several other open Android e-readers, I haven't been impressed. The Remarkable Paper Pro is way too big and the Boox Go is too slow and too difficult to get books on, so I wasn't expecting much from the Durobo Krono. Turns out, it is a phenomenal e-reader.

Recent findings suggest that since I test e-readers for a living, my digital library is spread out across all different platforms. Rather than balancing a bunch of different e-readers, the Krono puts both my Kindle and Kobo libraries on one device. The only library I don't have access to is Apple Books, since it's unavailable in the Google Play Store.

The Durobo Krono is the perfect size, with a 6.13-inch display, similar to the basic Kindle. It has a matte display with 300 ppi resolution. It also has a front light with adjustable brightness and warmth.

Sources indicate that powered by an octa-core processor, it moves promptly between apps and books. It easily competed with the speed of both Kindles and Kobos; however, it can get bogged down. It runs the Kindle app, Libby, and Libro.fm no problem. But some apps, like Substack, slowed it down with their high internet demands. Once I deleted the Substack app, though, it got back to normal.

As someone who loves to read while listening to the audiobook, I also love that I can do both on one device. I can listen to an audiobook on Audible while reading the EPUB file alongside it. The Krono also has voice transcription and note-taking capabilities, a nice bonus feature, but not essential in an e-reader.

Read our full review of the Boox Go 6 (Gen II).

You want an e-reader that does more: If you want to do more on an e-reader, like check your Storygraph or browse Libby, then you'll need one with an open system. The Boox Go 6 (Gen II) runs on an Android 11 system with access to the Google Play Store, so you can download any app to your e-reader. Yes, it could lead to more distractions, but with an E Ink display, it still feels more analog than a classic iPad or Android tablet.

Recent findings suggest that but you want it to look like an e-reader: The Boox Go 6 (Gen II) doesn't look like a tablet, though. The E Ink display provides a matte, black and white background with 300 ppi resolution, so it's gentle on the eyes. It's the same size as a basic Kindle but with the flush front design of a Paperwhite, so it gives you the best of both worlds.

The Boox Go 6 (Gen II) is the brand's answer to Amazon's Kindle. With a 6-inch screen, it fits comfortably in your hand for hours of reading. With an open Android system, you can download any app in the Google Play Store, so you can access any book across any app, including Kindle, Rakuten Kobo, and Libby.

Sources indicate that it's the perfect size and shape to hold for hours at a time. Boox even sells a MagSafe case so you can pop on a PopSockets grip for an ergonomic hold. Boox e-readers do have a bit of a learning curve, as the E Ink display requires a bit of tinkering. But once you get it set up, it's extremely customizable.

Industry observers note that because it can tackle a lot of apps rather than just doing one thing like a Kindle, it needs some extra power behind it. Unfortunately, it doesn't quite have it. The Boox Go 6 suffers from significant lag and screen response issues that make it occasionally frustrating to use. It's slower than either a Kindle or a Kobo, but it's a consolation you'll have to make if you want an e-reader that does more.

Miniature enthusiasts: If you want an e-reader that you can have on you at all times and even slip in your pocket, there are so few options out there. That's what makes the Xetink X4 so special. It's a truly tiny e-reader with a 4.3-inch display; but with a built-in magnet, it can attach to MagSafe devices so you can keep it attached to your iPhone.

You must love DRM ePUBs: If you think you're getting a mini Kindle, you're not. Instead, expect a tiny e-reader that is a great fit for turning online articles into PDFs or collecting all the free ePUBs. It's not compatible with any DRM files.

Recent findings suggest that in such a little package, the Xetink X4 feels like it should be a toy, but it's actually a solid e-reader. It's the smallest e-reader we've tested, measuring 4.3 inches, so you can slip it in your pocket and go. That small display, while convenient on the go, won't be suitable for all eyes, especially if you like to crank up the text size on your e-reader or phone.

Recent findings suggest that the resolution of the Xetink X4 is 219 ppi, which is lower res than you'll find on most e-readers. It also includes page-turning buttons along the bottom of the e-reader. Xteink has a great transfer system, too. It's similar to Amazon's Send to Kindle feature, in that you can send EPUBs and articles to the e-reader. The ability to send articles is particularly compelling, so you can send your reading list to your e-reader and enjoy them in one spot.

Industry observers note that my biggest problem with the Xetink X4 is how few files it supports, as you can't access Libby books or any DRM files on it. If you are going to commit, you'll have to be OK with reading primarily free EPUB files. However, folks at Lifehacker figured out how to install different firmware onto the device for a better reading experience.

Read our full review of the Kindle (2026).

Quality on a budget: If you want to dip your toes into e-readers, the standard Kindle model is the best budget-friendly model. Like the Paperwhite, it has 16GB of storage, with room for thousands of books. It’s the smallest Kindle, and you won’t miss the size of the Paperwhite. Instead, you’ll be delighted that it’s genuinely pocket-sized. Plus, if you want an e-reader with some flair, it’s now available in black and ube. Plus, the 2026 version even has two aluminum options in alpine sky or seaglass green.

According to recent reports, amazon made some updates to the 2026 Kindle that make it worthy of its higher price tag. It has a fresh, flush front design for a sleeker look. Plus, the design team made a change we've been dying for — they moved the power button to the side of the device. Plenty of specs have stayed the same between generations. It still has a 6-inch screen, 300 ppi resolution, and six weeks of battery life.

In a recent development, what truly makes it stand out is just how lightweight it is. The 2026 Kindle weighs 18 grams (.66 ounces) less than the previous generation and it's a noticeable difference. It feels like you're barely holding anything; plus, it's even better for travel as it takes up very little space and weighs just half a pound.

Industry observers note that it's a speedy little e-reader, too. Its screen is responsive and loads books within seconds. The only thing that could make the e-reader better is if Amazon added an adjustable warm light and made it waterproof. However, according to Amazon, the lack of those features keeps it affordable.

Recent findings suggest that the device is now available in its basic format in either ube or graphite. However, it's also available with an aluminum backing, making it more like a tablet. The aluminum Kindle is more expensive at $189.99, but it does come with 32GB of storage and two additional color options.

Read our full review of the Kobo Libra Colour.

Sources indicate that color enthusiasts and graphic novel readers: For serious readers who don't mind splurging a little, the Kobo Libra Colour delivers an upgraded e-reader experience. With a similar seven-inch display, the Libra Colour offers two features the Kindle Paperwhite cannot: Color and note-taking. Book covers, in-book illustrations, and photos are all featured in color with the Libra.

Recent findings suggest that annotators and highlighters: And if you're an annotator, you can highlight and mark up your pages in different colors to stay organized. In the Kindle family, only the Scribe supports scribbling, and with a higher price tag.

In a recent development, bathtub readers: It's equipped with more than enough storage at 32GB and is waterproof. Plus, if you were devastated by the discontinuation of the Kindle Oasis, the Libra Colour offers a similar design that includes page-turning buttons.

Recent findings suggest that if you were to ask me which e-reader to buy, it's a real toss-up between the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition and the Kobo Libra Colour. While the Kobo Libra Colour is expensive at $259.99, it's worth its price tag for all its included features.

Above all, the Kobo Libra Colour has the best ergonomic design. It's more square than a Kindle, as one side offers extra space for page-turning buttons. This makes it easier to hold, especially while lying down and reading one-handed. It's one of the few e-readers to have an internal gyroscope, so when you rotate the device, the display rotates with it. While reading in bed, if I flipped over, I could rotate the device to still be able to hold it on the side with page-turning buttons.

While the color display on the Kobo is nice, it is still rather muted. While reading Heartstopper, the colors were quite toned down in comparison to how they appeared on the iPad Mini. The Libra Colour's battery life isn't as strong as a Kindle Paperwhite's. While testing the Kobo Libra Colour over 10 weeks, my colleague Bethany Allard had to charge the device twice. Plus, it's a bit slower than a Kindle, with the occasional stall while switching between books.

Sources indicate that while the Kindle may have the Kobo beat on processing and battery life, I still think the Libra Colour is a worthy upgrade as it offers the best design of an e-reader with the perk of color. Amazon's color e-reader, the Colorsoft, costs $289.99, so at $259.99, the Libra is a little cheaper.

Recent findings suggest that young readers: If you're raising a voracious reader, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids is the best e-reader for kids. It's waterproof, which means it stands up to juice spills and dips in the pool. Plus, it comes with a built-in case. It's designed to be kid-proof, not just physically, but also with built-in parental controls. If you're concerned about monitoring your kid's bookshelf, this Kindle allows you to approve downloads by kids and displays age-friendly titles that kids can easily access.

Recent findings suggest that one area where Amazon has all other e-reader brands beat is in the kids market. There are special kid-friendly models of the basic Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft. Our preferred model for kids is the Kindle Paperwhite Kids.

More than anything else, an e-reader for kids has to be waterproof, which is why the Kindle Paperwhite Kids is the best choice. It comes with everything we like about the standard Paperwhite: a beautiful, high-resolution screen that works faster than any previous generation.

Sources indicate that but what makes it great for kids is that it's a distraction-free device. It doesn't come with ads, notifications, or the temptation of games or video. I also like that it's a bit heavier than the standard Paperwhite, giving it a sturdier design. Plus, the built-in case adds an extra level of protection.

Recent findings suggest that the parental controls are easy to use and set up, and the device also comes with a six-month free subscription to Amazon Kids+, which provides unlimited access to thousands of age-appropriate books. The library of books is easy for kids to navigate and offers classics like Lois Lowry's The Giver and modern classics like Diary of a Wimpy Kid.

According to recent reports, what I don't love is the price. At $229.99, it's more expensive than the standard Paperwhite. If you want to go for a budget kids' pick, I'd recommend the standard Kindle, which you can set up as a kids' device during setup to ensure parental controls and add an Amazon Kids+ subscription for $5.99 per month. Plus, as your kid ages, you won't have to upgrade to a more teen-friendly e-reader.

Read our full review of the Kindle Scribe (3rd Generation).

Sources indicate that for annotators and journalers: If, looking through your bookshelf, your books have dog-eared pages, highlighted lines, and scribbles in the margins, your instinct might be that an e-reader isn't for you, but I'd like to introduce you to the Kindle Scribe. It's the only Kindle with writing capabilities and comes with an included stylus pen that magnetically attaches to the side of the e-reader; it's ready for all your handwritten thoughts.

Sources indicate that the pen moves nicely across the screen, mimicking the texture of writing on paper. In addition to a library of books, the Kindle Scribe also comes with a journal section where you can take notes. The notes feature is especially great for students who want to handwrite notes and convert their handwriting into text.

The 2025 Kindle Scribe got a much-needed upgrade. All the good stuff has held over with the addition of some major improvements.

Industry observers note that it's still big, with an 11-inch display, which does make it a little more awkward to hold while reading, but for writing or annotating, it's optimal. Unlike other tablets (I'm looking at you, iPads) that require you to buy a pen separately, the Kindle Scribe comes with a pen that conveniently attaches to the side so it doesn't get lost. However, it's not the most secure magnetic hold, so be careful not to bump the pen off accidentally.

Recent findings suggest that writing on the Kindle Scribe is a joy. Before testing this e-reader, I used my iPad and Apple Pencil to annotate readings, but I never loved it because the screen felt too slick for the Apple Pencil. The Kindle Scribe does not suffer this problem, as the matte screen lends some friction to the pen, making it feel like you're writing on paper. I enjoyed writing with the pen, and I swear my handwriting looked better on the Kindle Scribe than on my iPad.

Recent findings suggest that it finally got a processing enhancement that makes it as speedy as every other Kindle. Gone is the lag when switching between journals and books. Plus, the displays have greatly improved, too, as the 2025 Kindle Scribe has virtually no ghosting. Like the Kindle Paperwhite, the Scribe's battery life lasts 12 weeks. It also has storage options, with 32GB and 64GB versions available.

According to recent reports, it's not your only option if you want a Kindle that can write. The Scribe Colorsoft is also available, and while we appreciate that model, it's quite a bit more expensive. The 2025 Scribe is a better value; it just doesn't have the wow factor of color.

Read our full review of the Apple iPad mini.

Sources indicate that single device users: There are so many devices that the modern person is meant to have. If adding an e-reader seems superfluous, I'd recommend a tablet that allows you to read books, stream demonstrates, and browse the internet. The best tablet for reading? It's the iPad mini.

According to recent reports, but why is this iPad better than any other? It's all about the size. At 8.3 inches, it comfortably sits in your hand and is about the same size as a paperback.

Sources indicate that before testing these e-readers, I read using my 9th-generation iPad, and my main complaint was always the size. After 30 minutes of reading, my hand and wrist would strain holding up all 10.2 inches of the screen. That's why the 8.3-inch display of the iPad mini was such a treat. Reading with the mini made me feel like I was holding an actual book rather than a laptop screen.

Recent findings suggest that unsurprisingly, the iPad mini has the most computing power of all the e-readers on this list. It jumps between apps and turns pages without an ounce of hesitation. Plus, it offers the most expansive ways to read books. You can read using Apple's built-in Apple Books app or download and read within the Kindle and Libby apps. And unlike most e-readers, you can read comics and graphic novels in full color. Plus, it has far more storage than any other e-reader, as the 7th generation iPad mini starts at 128GB of storage.

Industry observers note that despite my love of the iPad mini, I have some beef, most of which is with the screen. While I love its overall size, it has a substantial glare problem. I've found this to be true with any iPad I've read on; the slick glass screen has a glare in almost any environment. That's no surprise in the sun, but even at night, I found the screen to be a little too shiny, causing my eyes to have some trouble focusing. This does have a fix; if you want your iPad screen to look more like the matte of a Kindle, a screen protector such as Paperlike creates that effect.

It has been revealed that additionally, compared to e-readers, which provide months of battery life, the iPad mini only gets you hours. If you're reading for a couple of hours a day, you're probably only charging the iPad once a week, which isn't a big deal but certainly more than a traditional e-reader.

Topics Amazon Books iPad Kindle E-Readers.

According to recent reports, when picking an e-reader, price is always a consideration. However, almost all e-readers fall into the same price range. Kindle and Kobo e-readers both start around $149.99/$159.99, while the tiny Boox Picco is just $109.99. If you want handwriting capabilities, Kobo and Boox make the most affordable options, as Kindle's Scribes start at $500.

Remarkable PaperPro: Whenever you search for e-readers, Remarkable's tablets will always pop up in the search results, but unfortunately, it's hard to obtain ePUB files on the Remarkable. With Remarkable, you can access files within Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive. If you have any locked ePUB files — like from Libby — you won't be able to access them on a Remarkable tablet. So, after testing the Remarkable tablet myself, it proved to be a better document reader or digital journal than an e-reader.

Sources indicate that onyx Boox Go 7: While we love the Boox Go 6, we didn't love the Go 7. It's the same size as the Kobo Libra or Amazon Kindle, but it really lags on processing speed. Reading ePUB files from Libby required downloading the Adobe Digital Editions app onto the Boox Go 7, and there was significant lag when opening and closing the app. While it was an easier process than getting library books on a Nook, it was still a major pain compared to Kindle or Kobo's integrations. The Boox Go 7 lagged and took ages to load files. I was most looking forward to testing this Boox because of its page-turning buttons, but unfortunately, I found that they didn't work on my device.

According to recent reports, boox Palma 2: I loved reading on the Boox Palma. It's a really solid palm-sized e-reader with an open Android system, so you can download any reading app from the Google Play store, including Libby, Kindle, and Kobo. Unfortunately, the Palma 2 is being discontinued, and its availability is dwindling, which is why it's not included in this list.

In terms of major-name e-readers, you might notice one omission from this list: the Barnes & Noble Nook. I have tested this e-reader, and it was previously featured on this list. However, after testing more devices, it no longer makes the cut. In comparison to any of the Kindles or the Kobo Libra, the Nook has sloth-like performance, making it frustrating to use.

Sources indicate that plus, getting my library books onto the Nook was a nightmare, as it was a multi-step process that required downloading to a computer before uploading to a Nook. Its only redeeming quality was the buttons on either side of the device, which made page turning a breeze. However, unless you are a loyal buyer of Barnes & Noble books, I recommend steering clear of the Nook.

According to recent reports, once you get an e-reader, it's time to fill it up with books, and that doesn't necessarily mean spending money. In fact, you can load up your e-reader without spending a dime; you just need to be a bit resourceful.

Recent findings suggest that the best way to read nearly any book — a classic or hot fresh release — is with Libby. I have read hundreds of free books with the Libby app — I wouldn't have been able to test for this guide without it. It connects with your library card, allowing you to borrow from your local library's digital collection. Plus, both Kobo and Kindle have exceptional Libby integrations.

Another way to build your library is through Stuff Your Kindle Day events. These are 24-hour opportunities led by authors that make books discounted or free.

If you're a fan of the classics or looking to discover a treasure lost to time, an online resource like Project Gutenberg has more than 75,000 books in the public domain that you can download and read on an e-reader.

According to recent reports, the best Kindle is the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, dethroning the standard Paperwhite. Overall, it strikes the right balance of performance and value, while possessing everything we want in an e-reader. The standard Kindle is great for those on a budget, but it's not waterproof, and while the basic Paperwhite is always a favorite, the Signature Edition aluminum case and extra features make it the best e-reader you can buy.

Sources indicate that our two favorite e-readers come from Kindle and Kobo, but is one better than the other? It depends on what you're looking for. If performance is your primary concern, then a Kindle, specifically the Paperwhite, is better as it outperforms the Kobo Libra Colour in terms of speed when turning pages or loading books. However the Kobo Clara Colour measures up to the Paperwhite's performance.

In a recent development, if you're looking to de-Amazon your life, then a Kobo e-reader is the better e-reader. It offers all the things we like in a Kindle, such as Libby integration, adjustable brightness and warmth, a waterproof rating, and an overall better-designed package. While Amazon discontinued its Kindle Oasis, an e-reader with page-turning buttons, the Kobo Libra Colour has not abandoned this fan-favorite design. It also features an internal gyroscope so you can rotate the Kobo for a better ergonomic experience.

Yes, you can read on an iPad, and as an iPad reader, I highly recommend it. iPads come with the Apple Books app. However, other reading apps, including Libby and the Kindle app, give access to the world of books.

For this reason, I included an iPad in my testing. The iPad Mini made my list because it is the perfect size to feel like you're reading a paperback novel versus larger iPad models like the 9th generation, which feel like reading a clunky magazine.

Buying an e-reader is a far more significant investment than going to the bookstore. Plus, you still have to buy e-books. At first glance, it seems like an expensive adventure. Luckily, even with an e-reader, you can support your local library. With Libby, you can borrow and read audio and e-books from your local library and get them on your digital e-reader.

Libby has an iOS app and can instantly send books to your Kindle. If you don't happen to have a Kindle or iPad, you can still upload your library books through Adobe Digital Edition. Aka, you can still support your local library — and not pay a single penny to read a new book.

Sources indicate that I tested each of these e-readers over several weeks, reading at least one book per device in different environments. Here are the criteria upon which we decided this guide.

How easy was it to download and read fresh books from Libby or the Amazon store? Did the Scribe's stylus work smoothly? Is the user interface intuitive or was there a learning curve? I also noted which e-readers work best with Libby, for easy access to library books.

E-reader models vary wildly in price; I made sure to include affordable options as well as splurge-worthy models that are a good value.

This includes auto-adjusting displays for indoor/outdoor reading, warm light settings to block blue light, note-taking abilities, and page turn buttons for one-handed reading.

I made sure to pinpoint which models are waterproof for a worry-free outdoor reading experience as well as those better suited for children.

Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every one of 212 plant-based foods and drinks tested in a latest study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, raising questions about the potential health effects of regularly consuming these products.
  • In a recent development, researchers examined a wide selection of vegetarian and vegan products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives and dairy substitutes.
  • In a recent development, mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including molds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every one of 212 plant-based foods and drinks tested in a latest study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, raising questions about the potential health effects of regularly consuming these products.

In a recent development, researchers examined a wide selection of vegetarian and vegan products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives and dairy substitutes. They detected at least one of 19 mycotoxins in every product, and many contained multiple toxins.

In a recent development, mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including molds. They can enter the food supply when agricultural crops become contaminated during growing, harvesting, or storage.

Sources indicate that the investigation was led by scientists at the University of Parma in Italy, with contributions from Cranfield University. The researchers analyzed 212 products, including plant-based meat alternatives (PMBAs) and plant-based beverages (PBBs). The selection covered foods commonly found on supermarket shelves, such as vegan burgers, vegetarian chicken pieces, vegan sausages, and oat, almond, and soy milk.

In a recent development, although the findings highlight how widespread these naturally occurring contaminants can be, the researchers also identified an vital reassuring detail. Every product contained mycotoxin concentrations below recommended European Union guideline levels, which the team stated reflected the high food quality standards maintained by the UK food industry.

Why Plant-Based Foods Can Contain Fungal Toxins.

Many of the ingredients used to manufacture plant-based foods are particularly susceptible to fungal contamination. Grains, legumes, and seeds can encounter mold in fields or storage facilities, creating opportunities for mycotoxins to develop before the ingredients reach food manufacturers.

Unlike bacteria or viruses, mycotoxins are chemical substances produced by certain fungi. Their presence in food does not necessarily mean the product contains living mold, and detecting a toxin does not automatically mean the food is unsafe. The potential health risk depends on factors such as the type of toxin, its concentration, and how much a person consumes over time.

This distinction is especially vital for people who eat plant-based products frequently. Someone whose diet regularly includes meat substitutes, dairy alternatives, grains, and legumes may encounter these substances through several different foods rather than a single source.

Could Repeated Exposure Pose Health Risks?

While the concentrations detected in the UK products were below recommended EU guidelines, researchers say the potential effects of repeated exposure deserve closer attention.

According to recent reports, earlier studies have suggested that consuming small amounts of mycotoxins regularly may contribute to cumulative exposure and potentially increase health risks. In other words, assessing a single product may not provide a complete picture of a person's overall dietary exposure.

According to recent reports, eating one of these products occasionally is unlikely to cause problems based on the levels reported. However, a diet that relies heavily or exclusively on plant-based foods could involve repeated exposure to mycotoxins from numerous ingredients and products. Researchers say understanding the combined effects is crucial for evaluating possible long-term health consequences.

The severity of mycotoxin exposure varies depending on the compounds involved and the amount consumed. At sufficiently high or harmful exposure levels, certain mycotoxins can damage the liver and kidneys, interfere with normal immune system function, and increase the risk of cancer.

Sources indicate that the latest findings do not establish that the tested products cause these conditions. Instead, they provide information that scientists can use to estimate how much exposure consumers may receive through their diets and develop more accurate food safety risk assessments for the UK population.

Scientists Call for Better Monitoring of Plant-Based Ingredients.

Andrea Patriarca, Senior Lecturer in Mycology at Cranfield University, emphasized that mycotoxins are a natural part of the food environment and should not discourage people from eating a varied diet. Mycology is the branch of biology devoted to studying fungi, including molds and yeasts.

Sources indicate that "Mycotoxins occur naturally in foods and cannot be completely avoided. As consumers, we should not be frightened or deterred from enjoying a variety of products.

However, a significant concern arises when newly introduced foods enter the market, as there are currently no established regulations to monitor mycotoxins. We collaborate closely with various sectors in the food industry, from farmers to food companies, to help implement effective mycotoxin management integrated within food safety standards. The data from our research helps food safety organizations in assessing risks, particularly in complex multi-ingredient products.

Industry observers note that we are presently collaborating with the University of Parma to evaluate the risks faced by the population based on different dietary habits. Our aim is to advise policymakers and raise awareness among vulnerable consumers.".

In a recent development, the researchers are particularly interested in how food safety monitoring can keep pace with the growing range of plant-based products. Foods made from multiple ingredients present additional challenges because each component may introduce different contaminants, making overall exposure more difficult to assess.

Sources indicate that their work also underscores the importance of monitoring raw materials throughout the food production process. Identifying and controlling contamination before ingredients are combined into finished products could help manufacturers manage potential risks more effectively.

What the Findings Mean for Plant-Based Diets.

The discovery of fungal toxins in all 212 products highlights the importance of studying dietary exposure across multiple foods, rather than evaluating each product in isolation.

For consumers, the results are not a reason to abandon vegan or vegetarian foods. The concentrations measured were below recommended EU guidelines, and the researchers stress that mycotoxins cannot be completely eliminated from the food supply.

In a recent development, instead, the study points to the need for continued research into how different eating habits influence exposure, particularly among people who depend heavily on plant-based products. The University of Parma and Cranfield University are continuing their collaboration to investigate these dietary patterns, identify potentially vulnerable groups, and provide evidence that can inform future food safety policies.

The research, titled "Mycotoxin contamination in plant-based beverages and meat alternatives: A survey of the UK market," was published in the journal Food Control.

The study was conducted as part of the European Union-funded Horizon Europe FunShield4Med project (HORIZON-WIDERA-2021-ACCESS-03), Grant Agreement No 101079173.

Materials provided by Cranfield University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.
  • Industry observers note that that vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov.
  • Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.

Industry observers note that that vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas.

Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.

According to recent reports, "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk noted on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit.

He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX prepares to shift most Starship launches to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.).

Sources indicate that musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.).

The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle.

Before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions, and it had reflown a booster twice. But the tech giant had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly.

So snagging Ship on the first try was a very substantial deal, according to Musk.

"Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how crucial this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday.

Recent findings suggest that and SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has said that the company wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030.

This mind-boggling cadence will help the organization build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites, and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that.

Assembly of that newly introduced Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on Flight 14, which rolled out on Sept. 28, and repeated the feat on Flight 15.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.
  • In a recent development, “Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow.
  • A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

In a recent development, “Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”.

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Industry observers note that instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Sources indicate that yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

In a recent development, “I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a substantial fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”.

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” notes the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, massive mince dish.”.

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists.

Recent findings suggest that lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

Sources indicate that from such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:.

But mark the Rustic, haggis-fed/.

The trembling earth resounds his tread/.

Clap in his ample fist a blade/.

And legs and arms and heads will cut/.

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, remarked Howie, who estimates that his tech giant Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

Best Mexican food: 23 dishes to try.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie remarked.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”.

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Recent findings suggest that such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

Recent findings suggest that “Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”.

Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

Sources indicate that “I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old Latest Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”.

Recent findings suggest that after downloading Muse, Roberts, who had over 7,600 followers, entered the prompt: “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on instagram and can you unfollow them for me. ”.

It has been revealed that within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”.

Following the success of his November 7 cleanse, Roberts posted about it on X, offering instructions to his followers. Over the past several weeks, parallel scenarios have played out across X, Instagram, and Facebook, with consumers sharing tips on how to automate their unfollows with the help of Muse.

Industry observers note that X user @justdrmj posted about the trend the same week as Roberts, and nearly every reply shared a taste for trivial grudge-holding. For him it came down to one simple rule: “Why be a fan?” “i agree. reciprocity is key,” one person noted in response. “The way I just cleaned house,” added another. In a seeming outburst of celebration, one X user posted: “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG.”.

Even tech worker Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 Instagram followers, stated she wasn’t about to be “anybody’s fan,” noting in an Instagram video that she used the feature to suss out “people that I know in real life that have unfollowed me.” “I downloaded Muse just to do this only,” one person responded.

In a recent development, with social media rapidly evolving, there is no longer a unified consensus around etiquette. For some people, following others is an indication of friendship or simply a way to keep tabs on your latest crush. Others view it as more of a social obligation—you follow someone if they follow you, but the opposite is true as well.

Natalie Pennington, an associate professor who researches social connection at Colorado State University, wonders about the consequences of people gradually outsourcing small social decisions to technology.

According to recent reports, “It is probably at least partially a question of not wanting to deal with emotionally uncomfortable things,” Pennington notes. “This also strikes me as another example of information we don’t really need that social media can give us. There’s this data that exists at the platform level or would take a lot of effort to find out on your own, but now you can learn with the click of the button. But it doesn’t mean it is something you need to know.”.

In October, despite the seeming popularity of the feature, Meta removed an advertising campaign that promoted Muse with the promise that people could “see who unfollowed you each week,” Business Insider reported.

When WIRED asked about the reasoning behind Meta’s decision to remove the ad, the company did not respond to a request for comment.

According to recent reports, but Muse’s capabilities aren’t just being employed to even scores. Some people are using the assistant to streamline feeds that have become extremely cluttered over the years.

According to recent reports, elizabeth Brooks is a self-proclaimed “sweeper”—the term for a hobbyist who routinely enters sweepstakes and promotional contests—who, over the course of 10 years, had followed various accounts offering giveaways. Recently, she started prompting the assistant to bring her five profile links every few hours, no more than six times a day, for her to manually unfollow one by one. “Your following list can finally work for you instead of the other way around,” she wrote on Facebook.

According to recent reports, roberts, who joined Instagram in high school 15 years ago and calls the platform “my app of choice,” says people are becoming more intentional about their digital relationships and who they let into their online lives. But he doesn’t proposal on letting Muse make any more decisions about his social life, he says.

“Unfollowing is where I draw the line.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The Hunger Games” franchise has caught fire once again.

“Sunrise on the Reaping,” the sixth installment in the billion-dollar dystopian franchise, has defied expectations and opened to $120 million at the box office, nearly tripling the $44 million opening of the 2023 prequel “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.”.

Industry observers note that surely part of the success here is the Jennifer Lawrence factor: The star’s return (alongside Josh Hutcherson) was first reported by Variety nearly a year ago — and the duo’s reunion with fellow franchise veterans Woody Harrelson, Elizabeth Banks and Jena Malone at the film’s Newly introduced York premiere ignited seismic levels of buzz online. Related Stories More Than Half of Video Game Workers Laid Off Over the Past Two Years Are Still Unemployed, GDC Industry Report Finds Troy Baker to Receive Legend Award at 2027 New York Game Awards (Gaming News Roundup).

According to social media analytics firm RelishMix, ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ amassed a social media reach of 652 million. That doesn’t trail far behind the 680 million pre-opening reach of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” — and represents a staggering 66% jump from “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes’” 393 million (more on par with the pre-opening reach of Disney’s “Hexed” at 391.9 million).

Sources indicate that so, in today’s IP-fueled Hollywood landscape, the blazing success of “Sunrise on the Reaping” would light a fire under the asses of most studio execs to get a seventh “Hunger Games” movie on the calendar as swiftly as possible. While it’d be a fool’s bet to call this the definitive end of the franchise on the significant screen, the odds of Lionsgate gifting fans another movie announcement this holiday season aren’t exactly in our favor.

The key here is Suzanne Collins, who has maintained an active creative role in the franchise since the film rights to her planned trilogy were acquired for $200,000 in 2009. Collins co-wrote the screenplay for the first film and has remained deeply involved in each film, working closely with franchise director Francis Lawrence on everything from story development to reviewing final cuts.

In a recent development, after the Jennifer Lawrence-led saga concluded in 2015 with “Mockingjay — Part 2,” the franchise sat dormant until 2020 when Collins published “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.” The prequel, set 64 years before Katniss Everdeen entered the arena, explores how an 18-year-old Coriolanus Snow became the tyrannical president of Panem. Lionsgate adapted the novel into a 2023 film and remained in lockstep with Collins, announcing its adaptation of “Sunrise on the Reaping” on June 6, 2024: the same day Scholastic unveiled her latest novel.

At the “Sunrise on the Reaping” premiere, when the topic of a seventh “Hunger Games” movie came up, everyone from the franchise’s creative forces to Lionsgate’s top brass delivered the same message: We’re waiting on Suzanne.

Lionsgate chairman Adam Fogelson claims there won’t be another #TheHungerGames movie until Suzanne Collins writes another book, promising to “honor and respect” her as the franchise’s “creative architect.” pic.twitter.com/zgPh2Ddebu.

“She does not do anything in a frivolous fashion,” Lionsgate chairman Adam Fogelson told Variety at the “Sunrise on the Reaping” premiere. “When she believes she has an key story to tell, I believe she will write it and we will be the beneficiaries of it. But nothing I can say or do — nothing anyone could say or do — is going to shake her core fundamental desire to be inspired to write a great story.”Collins attended the “Sunrise on the Reaping” premiere, joining a behemoth group photo that brought together Lawrence and the vets who worked on the original four films, Rachel Zegler and the “Songbirds and Snakes” crew and the fresh crop of tributes from the latest installment.

The press-shy author didn’t give any interviews, but while signing autographs for fans, she offered an ambiguous two words when asked whether another novel was on the way: “We’ll see.” (Fans on X were considerably less restrained, with one parody account declaring: “SUZANNE COLLINS CONFIRMED A UPCOMING HUNGER GAMES BOOK”).

Perhaps the fans are right, and this is all one major game of Werewulf, but Lawrence insists that he hasn’t caught so much as a whiff of another book.

In a recent development, “I’m telling you — the studio doesn’t believe us, I don’t think anybody believes us — but she does not tell us a word,” Lawrence explained. “She gives us no hints if she’s writing or not.” The director added that he doesn’t think the studio is necessarily “comfortable” with the prolonged waits between Collins’ novels: “I think they wish that she’d just be pumping them out. But, you know, she does her thing. And that’s part of what makes them so great.”.

Whichever direction the franchise heads next, the numbers suggest there are limits to its appeal — and that not every trip to Panem is guaranteed to draw the same crowd.

Haymitch Abernathy’s origin story has struck a significantly stronger chord with the fanbase than President Snow’s, both on the page and on screen. “Sunrise on the Reaping” sold more than 1.2 million U.S. copies in its first week, twice the first-week sales of “Songbirds and Snakes” and three times those of “Mockingjay.” By January 2026, worldwide English-language sales had surpassed 4.4 million copies.

That success translated to the big screen: “Sunrise on the Reaping” currently holds the highest audience score on Rotten Tomatoes (94%) and Letterboxd rating (4.1/5) in the franchise, even surpassing the beloved “Catching Fire” (89% audience RT score; 4.0/5 Letterboxd).

It has been revealed that hollywood has also seen the pitfalls of stretching a franchise beyond its source material to capitalize on its commercial success. Most infamously, HBO forged ahead on a final season of “Game of Thrones” as George R.R. Martin struggled to complete his sixth “A Song of Ice and Fire” novel, culminating in a wildly divisive final season that prompted more than a million fans to petition for a remake. Martin later revealed in 2022 that he had been largely “out of the loop” during the show’s final seasons.

According to recent reports, “If you look at our relationship with Stephenie [Meyer] on ‘Twilight,’ Chad [Stahelski] and Keanu [Reeves] on ‘John Wick,’ or our longstanding relationship with the ‘Saw’ creators, this is a studio that has prided itself on making great content, but never underestimated how crucial it is that the architects of that creation continue to have a voice in the process,” Fogelson remarked, reaffirming Collins as “the creative architect” of the “Hunger Games” franchise. “We have made sure that she is a true partner with our studio across the board. And I think the movies, the campaigns, and everything we do are better for it.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” is playing in theaters now.

Recent findings suggest that the bill of fare has long had a dedicated section of “Bel-Air Classics”: the tortilla soup, the club sandwich, the chopped salad named for late No. 1 fan Nancy Reagan. Recent findings suggest that “When you go home, you want what you remember,” explains Hotel Bel-Air manager Tiffany Lai, who insists the restaurant’s back-to-basics pivot won’t condemn it to culinary ossification. “We’re still busy creating newly introduced favorites.” She points to the German-born, Austria-raised Schlegel’s signature dish: chicken schnitzel with lemon paprika (left). “Maybe in 15 years that’ll be the next classic.”.
